target_constraint: Must maintain glenoid fixation under rotational loads for 10+ years
observed_phenomenon: Glenoid component loosening causing pain and instability
mechanism: The evidence indicates that persistent pain after shoulder arthroplasty can be evaluated via diagnostic arthroscopy to identify mechanical causes (e.g., loosening) when conventional imaging is inconclusive, enabling targeted intervention before revision.
intervention: Integrate a diagnostic arthroscopy-guided cement augmentation protocol for cemented polyethylene glenoid components: when a patient presents with pain and suspected loosening but inconclusive radiographs, perform arthroscopic inspection to confirm mechanical loosening, then inject low-viscosity bone cement into the loosened glenoid-bone interface under direct visualization to re-stabilize fixation, avoiding full revision.
expected_effect: This intervention would extend glenoid fixation by addressing early mechanical loosening with a minimally invasive re-cementing procedure, potentially maintaining rotational load resistance for 10+ years without requiring component replacement, thereby reducing pain and instability.
falsification_test: In a cadaveric or biomechanical model, create a cemented glenoid with induced loosening, apply the arthroscopic cement injection, then cyclically load the glenoid under rotational forces (e.g., 10,000 cycles at physiological torque) and measure displacement; if the re-cemented glenoid shows >2 mm migration or fails before 10,000 cycles, the intervention is falsified.
source_spans: "The purpose of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic utility of shoulder arthroscopy in identifying infectious and mechanical causes of pain and to assess its impact on subsequent management decisions."
